nameStory: The word "corn" originally meant any grain crop in Old English, which is why Europeans called it "maize" using the indigenous Taíno word "mahiz." In North America, corn became the dominant grain, so the name stuck to this specific plant. That's why in England, "corn" still refers to wheat, but here it means this tall, golden grass!
description: Corn is a towering grass that can grow 6-10 feet tall with thick, sturdy stalks and long, sword-like leaves. The familiar ears of corn develop along the stalk, wrapped in green husks, while feathery tassels crown the top of each plant. Though we think of it as a vegetable, corn is actually a cereal grain - just like wheat or rice, but much bigger! Each kernel is technically a seed, tightly packed in neat rows around a central cob.

idTips.label: Tassels
idTips.description: Feathery, golden-brown flower clusters at the very top of the plant that release clouds of pollen when shaken - these are the male flowers

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, sword-shaped leaves with prominent parallel veins and rough edges that can actually cut skin if you run your finger along them carelessly

idTips.label: Ears
idTips.description: Thick, cylindrical structures wrapped in papery green husks, emerging from joints along the main stalk - peel back to reveal rows of kernels

idTips.label: Stalk
idTips.description: Thick, bamboo-like stem with visible joints or nodes, feeling solid and sturdy when you knock on it with your knuckles

idTips.label: Silk
idTips.description: Fine, thread-like strands (often yellowish or brown) emerging from the tip of each ear - these are actually the female flower parts

habitat: You'll find corn growing in cultivated fields, gardens, and farm plots throughout New England's valleys and flatter terrain. It prefers rich, well-drained soil and full sun, so look for it in open agricultural areas rather than wild spaces. Since corn can't survive without human care, any corn you see has been deliberately planted - it doesn't grow wild anywhere in New England.

seasonality.spring: Young corn plants emerge as bright green shoots in late spring, looking like thick grass blades pushing up through the soil in neat rows.
seasonality.summer: Plants shoot up dramatically, developing their full height, broad leaves, and distinctive tassels by midsummer. Ears begin forming along the stalks.
seasonality.fall: Corn reaches maturity with golden tassels releasing pollen, full ears ready for harvest, and leaves beginning to yellow and dry out.
seasonality.winter: In fields, you might see dried brown stalks and stubble left after harvest, or completely bare ground where corn once grew.

funFact: Every single kernel of corn on an ear is connected to one strand of silk - so an ear with 800 kernels has exactly 800 individual silk threads, each one a tiny flower that had to be pollinated to make that kernel develop!
confusionNotes: Young corn might be confused with other tall grasses, but corn's thick, sturdy stalk and the neat rows it's planted in give it away. Wild grasses grow in clumps or patches, while corn stands in soldier-straight lines across fields.
contextualKnowledge: Corn is completely dependent on humans for survival - it can't reproduce without our help because the kernels are too tightly attached to the cob to scatter naturally. This amazing grass was transformed by indigenous peoples from a wild plant called teosinte over thousands of years of careful selection.
compareHints: Corn is the only member of the genus Zea you'll see in New England, making it unique among our grasses. While other tall grasses like reed grass or wild rice might seem similar from a distance, corn's thick stalk, broad leaves, and distinctive tassels and ears make it unmistakable. Plus, its orderly rows in cultivated fields set it apart from any wild grass species.
